evidence: book(): converts form.startsAt to a Date, calls this.scheduling.book(...) and returns present(appointment), which is presentation mapping plus delegation
cancel(): calls this.scheduling.cancel(id, new Date()) and presents the result, so the cancellation rules stay in the business service
addNote(): calls this.notes.write(...) and returns { count } from notesFor(id).length, which only shapes the response
BookingForm / NoteForm interfaces are input DTOs, which are presentation concerns
parsedVerdict.reasoning: AppointmentsController does what a presentation-layer controller should. It defines input form shapes (BookingForm, NoteForm), turns form fields into service arguments (for example, it parses startsAt into a Date), hands the work to business services (SchedulingService, VisitNotesService), and formats responses through the presenter. It has no business rules such as overlap checks, validation of booking constraints, or cancellation policy. It also has no persistence or framework/transport logic. Two small points are still fine: cancel() supplies `new Date()` as the current time, and addNote() returns a count of notes. Both are request/response handling, not domain rules.
